The positive discrepancy therefore gives 66(n/99 − n/100) = 1/2, or n/150 = 1/2, so n = 75. The repeating fractional part follows either by multiplying by 100 and subtracting or by a geometric series with ratio 1/100, whose absolute value is less than 1. The modeling and denominator-clearing scopes are appropriate.

The common gcd of a, b, c divides both 23 and 9, so it is 1. Consequently, the three pairwise gcds are pairwise coprime. Their unordered positive values summing to 9 can only be (1,1,7) or (1,3,5). The first pattern gives (7,7,9); the other possible multiples-of-7 pair yields (2,7,14), which fails the required gcd pattern. The second pattern requires numbers at least 15, 3, and 5, so their sum forces (3,5,15). Thus the distinct square sums are 179 and 259, totaling 438. The supplied sorted-triple bounds also give a complete finite enumeration route.

Each ball has volume (4/3)π·2³ = 32π/3, while the cube has volume 216. Volume preservation bounds the number by floor(216/(32π/3)) = floor(81/(4π)) = 6. This bound is attained by reshaping each of six balls into a slab with base 6 by 6 and thickness 8π/27; their total thickness is 16π/9 < 6. Thus the extremal bound and construction are valid, and sphere packing is irrelevant. The numerical solution nevertheless requires an absolute sphere-volume formula whose catalog coverage has not been established from a supplied definition.

audits.mathematicalReason: The required region is |x| + |y| ≤ 20 with integer coordinates. The origin contributes one point. For each integer k from 1 through 20, the exact-distance boundary |x| + |y| = k contains 4k lattice points, including the axis endpoints without duplication. Hence the total is 1 + 4(1 + 2 + ⋯ + 20) = 1 + 4·210 = 841. Lattice counting is the assessed operation, and arithmetic-sequence summation appropriately supports the selected shell method.

routes.label: Bound the total using a nonnegative product

audits.mathematicalReason: Let the grid have r rows and c columns. Equality of interior and perimeter counts requires r,c ≥ 3 and 2(r−2)(c−2) = rc, equivalent to (r−4)(c−4) = 8. The admissible positive factor pairs are (1,8) and (2,4), up to interchange, giving totals 60 and 48. A 5 by 12 grid attains 60, with 30 interior and 30 perimeter pieces. The alternative bound is valid too: the equation and integer domain imply r,c ≥ 5, so (r−5)(c−5) ≥ 0, which reduces to rc ≤ 60.

routes.label: Lift one binary digit at a time
Recover a prefix using powers modulo 7

audits.mathematicalReason: Define C_n = (7S_n−1)/2ⁿ. Initially x_0 = 1 and C_1 = 3. The next bit is uniquely selected so C_n + 7x_n is even, with C_(n+1) = (C_n + 7x_n)/2. The carries cycle 3,5,6, producing the repeating bits x_1,x_2,x_3 = 1,1,0. Thus the four requested bits are 0,1,1,0, giving 6. The power-cycle route also works: 2²⁰²³ ≡ 2 modulo 7 gives S_2023 = (1 + 3·2²⁰²³)/7, and floor(S_2023/2²⁰¹⁹) = 6.

routes.label: Locate peaks and check nearby integers

audits.mathematicalReason: For n = ∏p^e, f(n)³ = ∏(e+1)³/p^e. For each prime, the ratio between successive exponent factors is ((e+2)/(e+1))³/p, strictly decreasing with e. The unique maximizing exponents are 3 for p=2, 2 for p=3, 1 for p=5 and 7, and 0 for every p≥11. Hence N = 2³·3²·5·7 = 2520, with digit sum 9. These independent strict maxima prove the global bound and its attainment. Adjacent differences give the same sign test; alternatively, 3ln(t+1)−t ln p has a single continuous peak, followed by comparison of the neighboring nonnegative integers.

After sorting the digits as b_1≤⋯≤b_5, the restrictions are exactly b_i<i, the successful linear-parking condition for five labeled cars and spaces 0 through 4. Instead park the cars on six circular spaces. Every one of the 6⁵ preference lists parks all cars and leaves one empty space. Rotation gives orbits of size six, each with exactly one representative whose sixth space is empty. Those representatives correspond to the required linear preference strings, so the count is 6⁵/6 = 1296. This symmetry acts on the auxiliary circular model, not on the original strings. Counting digit multiplicities by positional choices and cumulative-state recursion is also defensible.

Write p(x) = (x−h)²−d² with distinct roots r=h−d and s=h+d, where d>0. The equations p(x)=r and p(x)=s have disjoint solution sets. Exactly three real solutions require one level to equal the minimum −d² and the other to exceed it; necessarily r=−d². Thus h=d−d²≤1/4, uniquely at d=1/2. The root sum 2h is therefore uniquely maximized by p(x)=(x−1/4)²−1/4=x²−x/2−3/16, giving p(1)=5/16. At this polynomial the two levels indeed have one and two preimages. Both the quadratic-vertex route and the coefficient-discriminant bound are valid.

Let the original set have n elements, least value m, greatest value M, and middle-element sum U. Then U+m=32(n−1), U=35(n−2), and U+M=40(n−1). Subtracting the equal-sized totals gives M−m=8(n−1)=72, so n=10. Hence U=280, m=8, and M=80. The original sum is 368 and its mean is 36.8. A two-variable system is available after substituting M=m+72, so both proposed routes fit their scopes.

Represent each student's languages by a k-element subset of the total set of m languages. Because all subsets have the same size, the pairwise condition holds exactly when the subsets are distinct. For m≤8 there are at most C(8,4)=70 subsets of any one size, insufficient for 100 students. With nine languages, C(9,4)=126, so choose 100 distinct four-element subsets. Their union necessarily contains all nine languages, since omitting one would allow at most 70 such subsets. This proves both the lower bound and an attaining construction using the supplied combination scopes.

The permitted lattice vertices are the origin and its six neighbors at distance 1. Let O_n and R_n count valid n-step walks ending at the origin and on the surrounding ring, respectively, retaining only walks that have never exited. From the origin there are six ring moves; from any ring vertex there is one move to the origin and two to adjacent ring vertices. Thus O_(n+1)=R_n and R_(n+1)=6O_n+2R_n, starting at (1,0). The successive pairs are (0,6), (6,12), (12,60), (60,192), and (192,744). Therefore the probability is 936/6⁵ = 13/108. The two states retain all information needed for future valid transitions.
